title: The Hanged Man

seo.title: Destiny matrix 12 — The Hanged Man: meaning of the arcanum
seo.description: What 12 means in the destiny matrix: The Hanged Man is a pause, a different angle and giving something up on purpose.

meaning: The twelfth arcanum in the destiny matrix is the energy of the stop and of the changed angle. It is not about acting, but about what happens when acting is impossible: life puts a person on pause, turns them round and makes them see the same thing differently. Its main idea is simple — the winner is not the one who pushes hardest, but the one who agreed to hang upside down and watch the picture to the end.

The engine inside The Hanged Man is the clash between will and letting go. He keeps wanting to press harder, to speed things up, to take control back, yet it is exactly this grip that leaves him hanging. The energy is released only through giving something up on purpose: dropping the quick and the small for the real and the own. While a person holds on, they hang; the moment they open their hand, they fall forward and gain movement.

To be the twelfth arcanum is to live at a pace that a hurrying world finds alien. From the inside it feels like slowness and frequent idle spells, behind which the strong version does quiet inner work: the pause becomes a source of precise, hard-won decisions and of a rare view that people who answer at a run never get. The weak version turns the same pause into being stuck and a pretty name for doing nothing — years of waiting in which nothing was given away and nothing received.

The twelfth is easy to tell apart from the cards standing next to it, and the difference shows up in what it does with time. The eleventh, Strength, is in no hurry either, but its patience is an effort: it holds the lion and does not loosen its grip; the twelfth holds nothing — it lets go and asks you not to hurry with an answer. The thirteenth, Death, cuts off and shuts the door for good, while The Hanged Man does not shut it — he keeps it ajar and waits until it becomes clear whether to walk in. His strength lies neither in the blow nor in the ending, but in the ability to wait it out and turn the point of view around.

article.title: Arcanum 12 in the destiny matrix: The Hanged Man, the power of a pause and a fresh angle
article.short: 12 in the destiny matrix is the arcanum The Hanged Man, the energy of a stop after which a person sees the situation differently. Its key move is to let go where you want to push harder: to give up the quick and the petty for the sake of the real thing, willingly and knowing what you get in return. In the plus the twelfth arcanum gives staying power, an unconventional view and the ability to wait without panic; in the minus, a sacrifice that keeps a tally and waiting with no end date. Almost four people in five have this number somewhere in their reading, and most often it stands at the entry to the relationship line and the karmic tail — for one person in six.

seo.title: Destiny matrix 12: The Hanged Man — arcanum meaning and positions
seo.description: Destiny matrix 12 is The Hanged Man: the pause after which you see differently. Plus and minus, where 12 stands, love, money, four tails and compatibility.

sections.h2: What 12 means in the destiny matrix
paragraphs: The Hanged Man is the arcanum whose main event is a stop. The Magician starts, The Chariot drives on, The Tower collapses, and the twelfth does nothing — and that is its work. It describes a situation where the usual action has stopped helping: the project has stalled, the conversation has hit a dead end, there is no answer. The usual reflex is to push harder. The energy of 12 suggests the opposite: stop fighting what will not move and look at what can be seen from where you are. Often it turns out the person has been battering at the wrong door all along.

The second key word is exchange. Popular readings call 12 the energy of sacrifice, and that word misleads: sacrifice sounds like loss. For the twelfth it is a deal with deferred payment. A student gives up a summer for a degree, a craftsman gives up quick money for mastery, a parent gives up a career leap for a year with a child. As long as a person knows what they are giving and what for, they are in the strong version of the arcanum. When they give so as to present the bill later, the minus begins.

The third is a different angle. A person with a strong 12 notices what cannot be seen on the run: where the opponent is right, where the problem actually turns out to be the solution, what a failure saved them from. Hence the reputation for being a little otherworldly: they answer late, and not with what was expected, and a month later it often turns out they were closer to the heart of the matter than anyone.

Arthur Edward Waite, creator of the best-known tarot deck, insisted that this is a card not of martyrdom but of “life in suspension, but life and not death”. That is the key to the whole arcanum. To endure is to sit it out and stay the same. The Hanged Man’s pause changes the one who waits: you come out of it later, but with a different view.

And a short note for those who come from numerology: in the destiny matrix 12 is not reduced to 3. The method has 22 arcana, numbers up to 22 stay themselves, so 12 is always The Hanged Man and never “a three in another form”.

sections.h2: 12 in the plus and in the minus
paragraphs: The same energy produces two very different portraits. The difference almost always comes down to one thing: whether the pause has a deadline and the sacrifice has a price.

head: In the plus
In the minus
rows: waits without panic for the situation to ripen
waits for years, and nothing ripens
gives, knowing what comes back in return
gives so as to present the bill later
finds a way out that people in a hurry don’t see
feels misunderstood and right against everyone
calmly lets go of what isn’t theirs
clings to a lost cause and calls it loyalty
helps when asked
rescues when nobody asked, and takes offence at the ingratitude
tolerates uncertainty longer than others
hides a fear of deciding behind “it’s not time yet”

paragraphs: At work, a strong 12 is the one who, three hours into a crunch, asks: “Hang on, are we even fixing the right thing?” — and turns out to be right. A weak 12 is the one who has spent three years in a “temporary” post because “it’s too early to leave”, and who reminds everyone at every opportunity how much they have put into this company.

At home, the strong version is a person who lets someone close go through a crisis in their own way: doesn’t hurry them, doesn’t rescue them, but stays nearby. The weak one is the line “I gave my whole life for you…”, spoken after twenty years of silent concessions. Nobody asked for those concessions, and the bill for them comes as a surprise to everyone.

There is a third minus too, which Benebell Wen, author of Holistic Tarot, writes about: showy martyrdom, a person “preoccupied with appearing holy”. They get so absorbed in the role of the suffering righteous one that the goal everything was started for can no longer be seen behind it.
Three questions tell a pause from being stuck:

ol: **Does this pause have an end date?** The Hanged Man’s pause ends; being stuck doesn’t.
**What do I get in return?** If there is no answer, it is no longer an exchange but a loss.
**Did anyone ask me for this?** Help nobody asked for is most often presented later as a bill.

paragraphs: Sex plays no part in the calculation: a man and a woman born on the same day have the same numbers and the same arcanum. The difference lies in how other people read the pause. A man with a strong 12 more often hears “make up your mind”, “be tougher”, “what are you waiting for?”, and he has two bad ways out: break himself to fit someone else’s pace or hide the pause behind silence. The good way out is a third one — a calm that needs no proof. Such a man doesn’t get drawn into competing for the sake of competing, doesn’t decide on emotion, and spots the way out that the hurried walked straight past.

Twelve is a common arcanum: counted across all dates of birth from 1900 to 2026, it appears in the reading of 79.4% of people. But the meaning of the number is set by the place where it stands. Here are all the roles of 12 and how often it lands in each.

paragraphs: The most common place is point M, the entry to two lines at once: relationships and the karmic tail. Twelve can stand there only for people whose karmic task is The Chariot (7) or The Emperor (4), that is, arcana of movement and power. In such a chart the first reaction and the root pull in different directions: at the entry you want to wait and adjust, while the task demands that you lead and decide.

Three places can be checked without any calculation at all. Point A is the day of birth, so everyone born on the 12th has 12 as their calling card. Point B is the number of the month, so everyone born in December has spiritual task 12. Point C is the sum of the digits of the year, and it gives 12 only for 1902, 1911, 1920 and 2019. Among people alive today these are mostly children born in 2019; the next will be the children of 2028.

In the reading by decades, 12 in the calling card colours childhood up to age 10, in the spiritual task the years from 20 to 30, in the material task from 40 to 50, in the karmic task from 60 to 70. A year under the twelfth arcanum is a separate story: [what a year of The Hanged Man brings](/year/12).

sections.h2: 12 as the calling card: if you were born on the 12th
paragraphs: The calling card is point A, what people pick up in the first minutes of meeting you. In those born on the 12th it is usually a calm that is hard to knock off balance. The person is in no hurry to answer: first they listen, then they say something unexpected — off-script, but to the point. Next to them, other people’s haste suddenly starts to look like fuss.

The second trait of this calling card is an angle of one’s own. In an argument they don’t take anyone’s side straight away but look for what both sides have missed. That is why they get called in when things are tangled, and are not much liked in meetings that need a quick “yes” or “no”.

The flip side is the same manner. From outside, unhurriedness is easily taken for indifference, and giving way for agreement. The most common trap of a 12 calling card is to give way in silence and then feel hurt that nobody appreciated it. It works in the plus when the pause ends in words: “I’ve thought about it, and here is what I see.”

On the age scale the calling card leads the first decade of life. A child born on the 12th often lives at their own pace: hurrying them is useless — the harder you push, the slower things go. But whatever they work out for themselves, they understand more deeply than their peers.

sections.h2: Born in December: The Hanged Man in the spiritual task
paragraphs: Point B is the number of the month of birth, so everyone born in December has The Hanged Man as their spiritual task. That is no promise of endless pauses. It is an inner lesson: learning to let go of what cannot be controlled, and not to confuse humility with doing nothing.

Two lines start from B at once: the talent line and the sky line. So for those born in December 12 is a gift and a task at the same time. The gift is to see later than others, but deeper and more accurately. The task is not to turn that gift into an excuse for an endless “not yet”.

In the reading by decades point B covers the years from 20 to 30. For December-born people this decade is read through 12: what matters in it often ripens in pauses — in a year of “not sure yet”, in a job “for the time being”, in a long choice. For The Hanged Man such pauses are not lost years, as long as you come out of them with a new view rather than a feeling that life has passed you by.

sections.h2: 12 in relationships: coming close by waiting
paragraphs: Most often 12 stands at point M — for one person in six. This is the entry to the relationship line: what you do in the first weeks, when the other person starts to matter. The twelfth at the entry doesn’t storm the gates. It looks closely, adapts to the other’s rhythm, gives way in small things and waits for the partner to take the step.

In the plus this is a rare and valuable quality. It is peaceful to be near such a person: they aren’t pushed, and they don’t push. They accept the other whole, know how to listen and can see someone through a hard stretch without demanding an immediate return. Their love is proved by time.

The minus is the unspoken request. The person does everything for the other and silently waits for them to guess they should do the same in return. The other doesn’t guess — a tally builds up and is then presented all at once, and the partner genuinely cannot see where the grievance came from. The second version of the minus is a relationship on pause for years: “we’ll see”, “it’ll sort itself out”, “things will still change”. In love, a pause with no end date becomes waiting that changes nothing except your age.

Point M is also the entry to the karmic tail, so the first reaction here is double: part of it is your own, part is an old, learned script. Everyone with 12 at M has a tail that starts with The Hanged Man: [12-19-7](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/12-19-7) if the karmic task is 7, and [12-16-4](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/12-16-4) if it is 4.

Further along the line, 12 turns up in two more places. In the middle of the line, at the partner point, it speaks of the question that surfaces after two people get close — there is a separate reading on that, [12 under the heart](/encyclopedia/position/love_middle/12). At the crossing of money and relationships, point R, 12 shows the rules the union rests on: someone gives way and pays more without discussing it. In the strong version this is flexibility in a hard period — “I pull us through now, you do it later”. In the weak one it is an inequality both of them keep quiet about.

The working rule for 12 in relationships is to ask out loud. A short sentence — “it matters to me that you…” — takes away half the minus: waiting becomes an agreement, and the partner no longer has to guess.

Twelve appears in the karmic tail of 24.4% of people, roughly one in four. Only four of the twenty-six tails contain it, and in each The Hanged Man plays a role of its own. The first number of a tail is the entry to the script, the second is its mechanism, the third its root.

ul: **[12-19-7](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/12-19-7)** — The Hanged Man at the entry: sacrifice for a great cause and the expectation that it will be repaid with victory.

**[12-16-4](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/12-16-4)** — The Hanged Man at the entry: enduring and putting things off for a long time, though the crack has been visible for ages, until everything collapses at once.
**[9-12-3](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/9-12-3)** — The Hanged Man as the mechanism: an unspoken request that puts life on pause while waiting for someone to guess.
**[18-3-12](/encyclopedia/karmic-tail/18-3-12)** — The Hanged Man at the root: accepting a limitation without turning it into martyrdom.

paragraphs: The common thread in all four is the same: a person agrees to wait or to give without naming a price. How this circle works in each tail and how to get out of it is covered on their pages.

sections.h2: 12 in the money channel and “under the dollar sign”
paragraphs: In the money line 12 can stand at the entry L, in the direction R2 and at the crossing with relationships R — for 3.3%, 3.7% and 1.7% of people respectively. The middle of the line, R2, is what popular charts most often call the energy “under the dollar sign”.

What all three places share: money comes to 12 unevenly. Income arrives in waves with quiet months in between, and that is a property of the channel, not a fault. The twelfth gets paid for what needs a pause: depth, long projects, a solution where others have given up. Its field is research, complex cases, restoration, consulting, analytics, art. Hardest of all for it are fast sales and conveyor-belt work.

At the entry L, the twelfth’s first money step is immersion, not selling: money comes after the person has shown they see the problem more deeply than the rest. In the direction R2 income rests on an unconventional approach and patience — on a narrow niche, on things that pay off a year later. At the crossing R money meets people, and here the main risk for 12 is the price left unnamed: “I’ll do it, and we’ll settle up later.”

The minus of money 12 is working for an idea, free help that is later thrown back at the person who got it, and guilt when it is time to ask to be paid. The plus is not panicking in a quiet month and not grabbing at any money going.
Three rules for 12 and money:

ul: count income by the year, not by the month;
keep a reserve for the pauses instead of borrowing against future quick money;
name the price before the work, not after.

paragraphs: How the money line works as a whole is covered in the article [money in the destiny matrix](/encyclopedia/position/money).

sections.h2: The Hanged Man in a couple’s matrix
paragraphs: Compatibility in the destiny matrix is read from a third, shared matrix: the matching points of two personal matrices are added together and the sum is reduced to a number from 1 to 22. Yuliana Lisovskaya described the meanings of such a matrix in most detail in her book Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024). In her school, 12 in a couple is a quiet, attentive union: the partners give way to each other, know how to listen and often sense what is happening with the other even at a distance. The minus is a sacrifice nobody asked for, living for the picture, and one partner holding the relationship together with all their strength.

Twelve also often stands in the couple’s centre — in about one couple in sixteen, for example when the partners’ centres are 5 and 7 or 6 and 6. This describes an energy, not a verdict: the same 12 can be a quiet harbour or a quiet trap, and the difference is whether the two say out loud what they expect. Where else 12 stands in a couple’s matrix and what it means at each point is on a separate page about 12 in compatibility.

sections.h2: How to work with arcanum 12: five practices

ol: **A deadline for every pause.** Write down every “I’ll wait” with a date: until when you are waiting and what you will do if nothing changes. When the date comes, check whether the decision has ripened or it is time to act with what you have.

**The exchange, out loud.** Before giving up something of yours for someone else, finish the sentence: “I am giving up… for the sake of…”. If there is nothing to put in the second half, don’t give it up.

**Someone else’s vantage point.** Describe the stuck situation as another person in it would see it, and then as you will see it ten years from now. The twelfth arcanum is strong at shifting the angle, and this exercise switches that on deliberately.

**A step within a day.** Once the pause has given you an answer, take one small action the same day: an email, a call, an application. For 12, an insight without a step quickly turns into one more pause.
**A request instead of a hint.** Once a week, ask for something directly, without waiting for people to guess. For the twelfth this is the shortest road from sacrifice to exchange.

paragraphs: And the twelfth needs to rest in its own way. What restores it bears little resemblance to rest by the schedule: half a day with no goal, water, woods, a road with no set route.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man beside Strength, The Hermit and Death
paragraphs: Three arcana close to it in meaning help to pin 12 down more precisely.

[Strength](/encyclopedia/arcanum/11) is in no hurry either, but its patience is an effort: keeping a grip on itself, not snapping, standing firm. The Hanged Man holds on to nothing — he loosens his grip. The eleventh withstands pressure; the twelfth stops resisting it. When both stand in the same matrix, the result is a rare stamina for long waiting — [the combination of 11 and 12](/encyclopedia/combination/11-12).

[The Hermit](/encyclopedia/arcanum/9) withdraws of his own accord: he chooses silence so as to be alone with himself. The Hanged Man is stopped by circumstances, and his task is to accept the stop, not to arrange it. The Hermit retreats; The Hanged Man freezes in the middle of life, in full view of everyone. Together they make for a life that is slow and deep — [the combination of 9 and 12](/encyclopedia/combination/9-12).

[Death](/encyclopedia/arcanum/13) is the next card and an ending. 12 is the pause before the turn: the old no longer works, the new has not yet begun. Waite links them directly: after “the sacred Mystery of Death”, he writes, “there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection”. On the two together — [the combination of 12 and 13](/encyclopedia/combination/12-13).

Benebell Wen adds [The Hierophant](/encyclopedia/arcanum/5) to this row: he is the “orthodox, conventional, institutionalized approach” everyone accepts, and The Hanged Man is disagreement with it, for which a price has to be paid. That is her dramatic version, and not every change of view means conflict with the majority. But if 12 sits in a prominent position in your chart, the feeling “I see it differently from everyone else” is probably familiar.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man in Waite’s tarot: what the card shows and where the image came from
paragraphs: In classic tarot, arcanum 12 looks the way Pamela Colman Smith drew it for Waite’s deck (1909). A young man hangs by one foot from a T-shaped crossbar. His other leg is bent and tucked behind the first, so the legs form a cross — many see the figure 4 in it. His hands are hidden behind his back. A halo shines round his head. He wears a blue jacket, red trousers and yellow shoes.

Waite himself pointed out what to look at. The tree is alive, “living wood, with leaves thereon”. The face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”. The figure as a whole “suggests life in suspension, but life and not death”. He calls the gallows a Tau cross, and the position of the legs a fylfot, another, ancient hooked cross. Benebell Wen has her own reading of one more detail: the hands are hidden because “his ultimate offering to the world has yet to be seen”.

Then Waite does something rare for him — he rejects every other interpretation at once. The card, he writes, “has been called falsely a card of martyrdom, a card of prudence, a card of the Great Work, a card of duty; but we may exhaust all published interpretations and find only vanity”. His own answer is short and hazy: the card expresses “the relation, in one of its aspects, between the Divine and the Universe”. Whoever can understand that “the story of his higher nature is imbedded in this symbolism” will receive “intimations concerning a great awakening” and will know that after the Mystery of Death comes the Mystery of Resurrection.

In the divinatory part of the book Waite’s list is more down to earth: “Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy.” Reversed: “Selfishness, the crowd, body politic.” That makes a curious pair: the upright Hanged Man sees differently from everyone, while the reversed one becomes the crowd himself. The destiny matrix has no reversed positions: a calculated number cannot be turned upside down, so there is no need to split 12 into “upright” and “reversed”.

The image itself is four and a half centuries older than Waite, and it started out with the opposite meaning. In fifteenth-century Italy this was how traitors were shown: under the custom of “defamatory painting” (pittura infamante), traitors hung by one foot were painted on the walls of public buildings. In 1440 Andrea del Castagno painted the Albizzi rebels on the façade of the Bargello palace in Florence and was nicknamed “Andrea of the Hanged Men”. In 1478 the same job went to Botticelli — this time with the Pazzi conspirators. Early Italian decks such as the mid-fifteenth-century Visconti–Sforza show the same figure, and in Italy the card was called “the Traitor”, il Traditore.

Then the meaning turned round. Court de Gébelin, an eighteenth-century French scholar, believed the figure should be turned the other way up: then it is Prudence, a man standing carefully on one leg and choosing where to put the other. Éliphas Lévi saw in the card “the adept bound by his engagements”. Waite rejected both readings, and on Pamela Colman Smith’s card the Hanged Man has a shining halo. The pillory had become an initiation.

Later interpreters compare The Hanged Man with Odin in the Norse Hávamál, the “Sayings of the High One”: the god hung on a tree for nine nights, offered up “myself to myself”, and at the end he saw the runes. There is no direct link to the card, but the meaning is the same: give yourself up for a while in order to see what you would not see any other way.

And one last detail that Wen notices. The dancer on the final card, The World, crosses her legs just as The Hanged Man does. Wen reads this as a promise: the completeness of The World comes to the one who has endured their own suspension. And The World’s number, 21, is 12 read from right to left.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: The meaning of the card follows Arthur Edward Waite’s The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen’s Holistic Tarot (2015). Where an idea belongs to an author, the text says so; the links to positions in the matrix are our own work.

Compatibility follows Yuliana Lisovskaya’s book Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024), retold in our own words. The book describes possible expressions of the energy, not conclusions about a particular couple.

The calculation is Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme. The shares of people were counted by going through every date of birth from 1 January 1900 to 2026; sex plays no part in the formulas.
The destiny matrix is a system of interpretation: it describes tendencies and suggests questions to ask yourself, but it does not predict events.
